title: The Innovator's Dilemma / Disruptive Innovation (Christensen)
pub: Christensen, The Innovator's Dilemma (Harvard Business School Press, 1997). Origin: Bower & Christensen, "Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave," Harvard Business Review 73(1) (Jan–Feb 1995): 43–53. Restatement: Christensen, Raynor & McDonald, "What Is Disruptive Innovation?" Harvard Business Review 93(12) (Dec 2015): 44–53.
author: Clayton M. Christensen · Joseph L. Bower · Michael E. Raynor · Rory McDonald

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Disruption theory: Historical examples weakly fit predictions
st.an: The source rejects the cluster’s central assessment of weak empirical fit by claiming broad cross-industry validation and significantly improved predictive accuracy. Its acknowledgments that disruption is narrowly defined and not a universal theory qualify its scope but do not concede the historical-testing critique.
qs: The key elements of that theory have been tested and validated through studies of many industries, including retail, computers, printing, motorcycles, cars, semiconductors, cardiovascular surgery, management education, financial services, management consulting, cameras, communications, and computer-aided design software.
But there is cause for hope: Empirical tests show that using disruptive theory makes us measurably and significantly more accurate in our predictions of which fledgling businesses will succeed.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Christensen offers a compatible general-management account in which technology’s effects depend on strategic deployment, business models and organisational structure. However, the source does not address legal AI’s jagged task-level capability, user expertise, verification or human-led work allocation directly, so it cannot establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: ## What a Disruptive Innovation Lens Can Reveal  It is rare that a technology or product is inherently sustaining or disruptive.
This was achieved not merely through product improvements but also through the introduction of a new business model.

st.t: Business disruption: Incumbents must separate experiments credibly
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: disruption is a business-model and market trajectory rather than an automatic effect of technology adoption. It also endorses sustaining the profitable core while pursuing disruptive opportunities through a separate operation, with cannibalisation addressed only if it materialises.
qs: Disrupters tend to focus on getting the business model, rather than merely the product, just right.
Our research suggests that the success of this new enterprise depends in large part on keeping it separate from the core business.

mo.t: Institutional reform: Outsider ideas need insider adoption

kp.k: Disruption is a specific process, not any market upheaval
kp.d: The authors define disruption as a smaller, less-resourced entrant establishing a foothold among overlooked customers, then improving sufficiently to attract mainstream customers while retaining its original advantages. They argue that applying the label to every industry-changing innovation obscures strategically important distinctions. This is a cross-domain management framework, not an analysis of AI or legal services.
qs: “Disruption” describes a process whereby a smaller company with fewer resources is able to successfully challenge established incumbent businesses.
When mainstream customers start adopting the entrants’ offerings in volume, disruption has occurred.
The problem with conflating a disruptive innovation with any breakthrough that changes an industry’s competitive patterns is that different types of innovation require different strategic approaches.

kp.k: Disruption starts in low-end or new-market footholds
kp.d: Low-end disruption serves less-demanding customers whose requirements incumbents have overshot; new-market disruption turns nonconsumers into consumers. The authors illustrate the latter with personal copiers introduced in the late 1970s, which offered affordable copying to individuals and small organizations before expanding into Xerox’s mainstream market. These are distinct entry mechanisms rather than interchangeable descriptions of cheaper products.
qs: Disruptive innovations originate in low-end or new-market footholds.
In fact, incumbents’ offerings often overshoot the performance requirements of the latter.
Put simply, they find a way to turn nonconsumers into consumers.
A disruptive innovation, by definition, starts from one of those two footholds.

kp.k: Sustaining innovation improves offerings for incumbents’ existing customers
kp.d: Sustaining innovations can be incremental or major breakthroughs. Disruptive offerings, by contrast, are initially regarded as inferior by most incumbent customers, who generally switch only after quality meets their requirements. The authors identify the combination of improved quality and retained lower prices as the mechanism through which disruption reduces market prices.
qs: These improvements can be incremental advances or major breakthroughs, but they all enable firms to sell more products to their most profitable customers.
Disruptive innovations, on the other hand, are initially considered inferior by most of an incumbent’s customers.
Instead, they wait until its quality rises enough to satisfy them.
Once that’s happened, they adopt the new product and happily accept its lower price.

kp.k: Uber’s taxi entry is classified as sustaining
kp.d: Writing in 2015, the authors argue that Uber entered an already-served mainstream taxi market rather than beginning with low-end customers or nonconsumers. Its convenience and service quality were generally considered superior, prompting incumbent responses. They treat Uber’s success as an outlier to the theory’s expectations for sustaining entrants and suggest, rather than establish, that taxi regulation constrained competitive responses.
qs: Uber has gone in exactly the opposite direction: building a position in the mainstream market first and subsequently appealing to historically overlooked segments.
Most of the elements of Uber’s strategy seem to be sustaining innovations.
According to disruption theory, Uber is an outlier, and we do not have a universal way to account for such atypical outcomes.
In Uber’s case, we believe that the regulated nature of the taxi business is a large part of the answer.

kp.k: Disruptive classification depends on the market being challenged
kp.d: The authors distinguish Uber’s taxi business from its potential trajectory in limousine services. In their 2015 account, UberSELECT offered lower prices than traditional limousines but lacked advance reservations, appealing to customers willing to sacrifice convenience. They condition its potential mainstream disruption on matching incumbent performance without losing cost and price advantages.
qs: The limousine or “black car” business is a different story, and here Uber is far more likely to be on a disruptive path.
Consequently, this offering from Uber appeals to the low end of the limousine service market: customers willing to sacrifice a measure of convenience for monetary savings.

Should Uber find ways to match or exceed incumbents’ performance levels without compromising its cost and price advantage, the company appears to be well positioned to move into the mainstream of the limo business—and it will have done so in classically disruptive fashion.

kp.k: Disruption unfolds over time and may remain incomplete
kp.d: The relevant unit of analysis is the offering’s trajectory, not its characteristics at a single moment. Disruption can erode market share and then profitability over decades, while incumbents continue earning incremental profits from older models. The authors use Netflix’s evolution from its 1997 mail-delivery service to streaming to explain how an initially peripheral offering eventually challenged Blockbuster’s core business.
qs: The term “disruptive innovation” is misleading when it is used to refer to a product or service at one fixed point, rather than to the evolution of that product or service over time.
Complete substitution, if it comes at all, may take decades, because the incremental profit from staying with the old model for one more year trumps proposals to write off the assets in one stroke.

If Netflix had not eventually begun to serve a broader segment of the market, Blockbuster’s decision to ignore this competitor would not have been a strategic blunder: The two companies filled very different needs for their (different) customers.

kp.k: Business-model differences can matter more than product improvements
kp.d: The authors contrast general practitioners’ experience-based diagnostic work with convenient care clinics using standardized protocols for a limited but expanding set of disorders. They also classify the iPhone initially as sustaining relative to smartphones but subsequently as disruptive relative to laptops as internet-access devices, attributing the latter trajectory partly to its developer-user network.
qs: Disrupters tend to focus on getting the business model, rather than merely the product, just right.
They follow standardized protocols to diagnose and treat a small but increasing number of disorders.

The product that Apple debuted in 2007 was a sustaining innovation in the smartphone market: It targeted the same customers coveted by incumbents, and its initial success is likely explained by product superiority.
By building a facilitated network connecting application developers with phone users, Apple changed the game.

kp.k: A disruptive trajectory does not guarantee commercial success
kp.d: The authors reject defining disruption retrospectively by success. They cite late-1990s internet retailers as examples of businesses pursuing disruptive paths with differing outcomes. The theory offers limited guidance on winning within a foothold market, beyond avoiding direct competition with better-resourced incumbents; successful platform businesses therefore need not represent a common disruptive strategy.
qs: But success is not built into the definition of disruption: Not every disruptive path leads to a triumph, and not every triumphant newcomer follows a disruptive path.
For example, any number of internet-based retailers pursued disruptive paths in the late 1990s, but only a small number prospered.
The theory says very little about how to win in the foothold market, other than to play the odds and avoid head-on competition with better-resourced incumbents.

kp.k: Incumbents should protect cores while exploring separate disruptive businesses
kp.d: The authors recommend continuing sustaining investment and core-customer relationships rather than dismantling a profitable business in anticipation of disruption. They suggest a separate division to pursue disruptive opportunities, while acknowledging that separation and senior leadership protection do not universally succeed and that managing incumbent and entrant operations simultaneously remains incompletely understood.
qs: Incumbent companies do need to respond to disruption if it’s occurring, but they should not overreact by dismantling a still-profitable business.
Our research suggests that the success of this new enterprise depends in large part on keeping it separate from the core business.
Sometimes this works—and sometimes it doesn’t.
The challenges that arise from being an incumbent and an entrant simultaneously have yet to be fully specified; how best to meet those challenges is still to be discovered.

kp.k: Head-on sustaining entrants face strong incumbent resistance
kp.d: The theory predicts that incumbents confronted with superior offerings aimed at their existing customers will accelerate innovation, defeat entrants, or acquire them. The authors cite Christensen’s disk-drive study, in which only 6% of sustaining entrants succeeded, without supplying a sample size or detailed methodology here. They emphasize that technologies are rarely inherently disruptive or sustaining: strategic deployment matters.
qs: It is rare that a technology or product is inherently sustaining or disruptive.

The theory of disruption predicts that when an entrant tackles incumbent competitors head-on, offering better products or services, the incumbents will accelerate their innovations to defend their business.
In Christensen’s seminal study of the disk drive industry, only 6% of sustaining entrants managed to succeed.

kp.k: Customer dependence institutionalizes incumbent resource-allocation priorities
kp.d: The authors explain incumbent underreaction through dependence on existing customers and internal processes favoring high-margin sustaining investments in large, familiar markets. They report interviews with disk-drive managers showing that these priorities starved disruptive opportunities serving small markets with poorly defined customers. They present this mechanism as part of the theory’s development from correlation toward causation.
qs: First, researchers realized that a company’s propensity for strategic change is profoundly affected by the interests of customers who provide the resources the firm needs to survive.
Incumbents’ focus on their existing customers becomes institutionalized in internal processes that make it difficult for even senior managers to shift investment to disruptive innovations.

For example, interviews with managers of established companies in the disk drive industry revealed that resource allocation processes prioritized sustaining innovations (which had high margins and targeted large markets with well-known customers) while inadvertently starving disruptive innovations (meant for smaller markets with poorly defined customers).

kp.k: Competition within footholds pushes surviving entrants upmarket
kp.d: The authors argue that multiple entrants often initially benefit from incumbents’ higher prices. As incumbents abandon the foothold, that price umbrella disappears and entrants face price-based competition. Some fail, while others improve their offerings and move toward higher-cost incumbents, creating pressure for both incumbents and entrants to move upmarket.
qs: The incumbents provide a de facto price umbrella, allowing many of the entrants to enjoy profitable growth within the foothold market.
As incumbents (rationally, but mistakenly) cede the foothold market, they effectively remove the price umbrella, and price-based competition among the entrants reigns.
The disruptive effect drives every competitor—incumbent and entrant—upmarket.

kp.k: Higher education illustrates limits of incumbent-emulating entrants
kp.d: The authors describe more than 100 years of new US higher-education institutions serving different populations, including nonconsumers, without substantially changing institutional rankings. They argue that entrants’ pursuit of prestige through costly imitation of elite institutions helped preserve incumbents’ positions. Online learning is presented in 2015 as a possible means of moving upmarket without reproducing incumbent costs, not as an established completed disruption.
qs: With few exceptions, the top 20 are still the top 20, and the next 50 are still in that second tier, decade after decade.
Because both incumbents and newcomers are seemingly following the same game plan, it is perhaps no surprise that incumbents are able to maintain their positions.
The question now is whether there is a novel technology or business model that allows new entrants to move upmarket without emulating the incumbents’ high costs—that is, to follow a disruptive path.
The answer seems to be yes, and the enabling innovation is online learning, which is becoming broadly available.

kp.k: Enabling technology affects disruption’s speed, not underlying mechanisms
kp.d: The authors link the slope of improvement trajectories to the rate of enabling technological progress. They contrast Nucor taking more than 40 years to match the revenue of the largest integrated steelmakers with Compaq increasing revenue more than tenfold and reaching parity with DEC in only 12 years. They argue that faster disruption does not require conceptually different responses.
qs: We’ve come to realize that the steepness of any disruptive trajectory is a function of how quickly the enabling technology improves.

In contrast, the digital technologies that allowed personal computers to disrupt minicomputers improved much more quickly; Compaq was able to increase revenue more than tenfold and reach parity with the industry leader, DEC, in only 12 years.
Rapid disruptions are not fundamentally different from any others; they don’t have different causal mechanisms and don’t require conceptually different responses.

kp.k: Tesla illustrates a conditional prediction about high-end entry
kp.d: In 2015, the authors classify Tesla’s foothold among customers willing to spend $70,000 or more as high-end entry attracting incumbent attention, rather than disruption. Conditional on their theory being correct, they predict acquisition by a larger incumbent or a prolonged struggle for market significance. This is a contemporaneous prediction, not a reported outcome.
qs: But its foothold is in the high end of the auto market (with customers willing to spend $70,000 or more on a car), and this segment is not uninteresting to incumbents.
If disruption theory is correct, Tesla’s future holds either acquisition by a much larger incumbent or a years-long and hard-fought battle for market significance.

kp.k: Authors claim empirical support while acknowledging explanatory limits
kp.d: The authors assert that key causal elements have been tested across numerous industries and that empirical tests show improved predictions of fledgling business success, but provide no effect sizes or methodological detail for those assertions here. They explicitly deny that disruption theory explains all innovation or business success and acknowledge unresolved questions about effective incumbent responses.
qs: The key elements of that theory have been tested and validated through studies of many industries, including retail, computers, printing, motorcycles, cars, semiconductors, cardiovascular surgery, management education, financial services, management consulting, cameras, communications, and computer-aided design software.
Disruption theory does not, and never will, explain everything about innovation specifically or business success generally.
Empirical tests show that using disruptive theory makes us measurably and significantly more accurate in our predictions of which fledgling businesses will succeed.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Christensen, Raynor and McDonald describe disruption as a conditional market-entry and upmarket-growth process, not as a synonym for technological improvement or commercial success.
pts.d: The supplied source is their December 2015 restatement, not the 1995 article or 1997 book. It makes no claims about AI or legal services. In its own cross-industry domain, the authors argue that entrants gain low-end or new-market footholds by serving customers incumbents overserve or overlook. Incumbents prioritize more profitable customers and initially respond weakly. Entrants that improve sufficiently while retaining their original advantages can win mainstream customers, reducing incumbents' market share and then profitability. New-market disruption turns nonconsumers into consumers; low-end disruption serves existing customers with a good-enough offering. Lower prices alone do not generally induce mainstream adoption before quality meets customer requirements.

pts.k: The authors predict stronger incumbent resistance to head-on sustaining entrants and explain upmarket movement through resource allocation and competitive pressure.
pts.d: They argue that existing customer interests become embedded in incumbent investment processes, favoring sustaining improvements over small, uncertain disruptive markets. When incumbents retreat from foothold markets, competition among entrants intensifies, encouraging surviving entrants to improve and move upmarket. Conversely, entrants directly offering superior products to incumbents' core customers should expect defensive innovation, defeat or acquisition. The authors classify Uber as sustaining relative to taxis and treat its success as an outlier, tentatively explained by regulatory constraints on incumbent innovation. They classify Tesla's high-end entry as sustaining and predict acquisition or a prolonged competitive struggle.

pts.k: Disruptive potential depends on the target market and business model; the authors identify conditional opportunities in limousine services and online education.
pts.d: The authors suggest UberSELECT could disrupt traditional limousine services if it closes performance gaps while preserving its cost and price advantage. They propose that online learning could allow education entrants to move upmarket without reproducing incumbents' high costs, citing falling real tuition and improving accessibility and quality. They distinguish business-model changes from product improvements: convenient care clinics use standardized processes rather than physicians' experience-based solution shops; the iPhone was sustaining against smartphones but, in their account, subsequently disruptive against laptops as an internet-access device through its application ecosystem. They advise incumbents to maintain profitable core businesses while exploring disruption through separate operations, but do not claim this response always succeeds.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Support combines an explicitly reported disk-drive statistic, managerial interviews, historical case narratives and broader claims of empirical validation.
pts.d: The authors report that only 6% of sustaining entrants succeeded in Christensen's disk-drive study, without supplying the sample size, study period or definition of success in this text. Interviews with disk-drive managers support their resource-allocation explanation. Historical illustrations include personal copiers expanding beyond Xerox's corporate clientele, Netflix's transition from mail-order DVDs to streaming and Blockbuster's collapse, and differing growth trajectories of Nucor and Compaq. They assert validation across numerous industries and improved predictive accuracy from empirical tests, but do not provide test designs, effect sizes or detailed results here. Uber's regulatory explanation is explicitly presented as their belief; online education and UberSELECT are forward-looking applications rather than demonstrated future outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The predictions are situated in 2015, concern trajectories rather than instantaneous changes, and carry explicit limits on timing, success and explanatory scope.
pts.d: Disruption requires a low-end or new-market origin followed by improvement sufficient for mainstream adoption while retaining early advantages. Complete substitution is neither immediate nor assured. The authors link the speed of disruption to improvement in enabling technology, contrasting Nucor's more-than-40-year path to revenue parity with major integrated steelmakers against Compaq's 12-year path to parity with DEC. They give no date for online education to disrupt incumbents or for UberSELECT to reach the limousine mainstream. Tesla's forecast is conditional on the theory and allows a years-long struggle. Disruptive entrants can fail; the theory says little about winning the initial foothold. Separate incumbent divisions are a qualified recommendation rather than a universally effective remedy.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects concern underserved and mainstream customers, resource-constrained entrants, incumbent firms and strategic decision-makers across industries.
pts.d: Low-end customers gain more suitable, often cheaper offerings; previously excluded individuals and small organizations gain access to products or services. Mainstream customers may later obtain acceptable quality at lower prices. Incumbents can lose share and profitability despite rationally prioritizing existing customers, while entrants face both foothold competition and incumbent resistance when competing head-on. Managers risk choosing inappropriate strategies if they label every successful innovation disruptive. Sector-specific affected groups include taxi and limousine operators and riders, traditional higher-education institutions and prospective students, health-care practices and clinics, and computing and retail businesses. These are the authors' cross-domain claims, not evidence of effects on lawyers, legal-service buyers or access to justice.
